source_document.body:
GLASGOW, Scotland — Russia may place a satellite loaded with a nuclear weapon into orbit by the end of the year, German public media reported, citing intelligence sources.
The satellite, dubbed Sputnik-S, has reportedly been assembled and stored in the greater Moscow area for several years. An investigation by German public broadcasters WDR and NDR and German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung uncovered an intelligence assessment from early November that says the satellite could be launched “within 60 days.”
Asked about the reporting during a visit to Berlin, NATO chief Mark Rutte said on Monday that the alliance was constantly assessing its deterrence and defence situation.
“I can assure you, we will always make sure that we defend every inch of NATO territory. And that includes making sure that we are safe when it comes to the space element,” Rutte told reporters at a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Placing a nuclear weapon in orbit is prohibited by the 1967 Outer Space Treaty, to which Russia and 117 other countries are parties.
Detonating an atomic bomb in space can have devastating effects: It is likely to destroy or incapacitate a large number of satellites, as well as cripple communications systems and power grids back on Earth with its electromagnetic pulse.
Both the United States and the Soviet Union detonated nuclear weapons in space during the Cold War, most significantly the American Starfish Prime test, 400 kilometers over the Pacific Ocean in 1962. The resulting artificial radiation belt damaged several satellites, including the Telstar-1 satellite launched a day after the blast.
Reporting by Western intelligence agencies of alleged Russian plans to place a nuke into orbit dates back several years. In early 2024, then-House Intelligence Committee chairman Mike Turner (R-Ohio) publicly warned of a “serious national security threat” without identifying it; U.S. media soon reported this was referring to a Russian space nuke. The U.S. intelligence community reportedly started circulating corresponding warnings a year earlier, in February 2023, German public media reports.
Shortly before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a mysterious satellite called simply Kosmos-2553 was launched, which Western governments had flagged as a potential space threat. Kosmos is the generic identifier for unnamed Russian satellites, including military ones with undisclosed functions.
The Russian authorities said Kosmos-2553 was for scientific research into radiation. However, Western intelligence agencies were “greatly skeptical” of this civilian explanation, according to the new reporting by German media.
Security services told WDR and NDR that they believe the satellite was being used to test the effects of nuclear weapons use in space. According to them, the satellite “functions as a so-called dummy, intended to test how radiation affects satellites – and at what point a satellite sustains severe damage.” The aim of the tests was to determine the extent to which the satellite remains operational and maneuverable under intense radiation.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin said it had no information on the topic, and said it rejected all accusations regarding the space activities of the Russian Federation, calling them part of a “propaganda campaign,” reporters from WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung wrote. Russian measures for the exploration and utilization of space are conducted in accordance with international commitments and “exclusively for peaceful purposes,” the Embassy said.
With reporting by Reuters
